bindingDocumentation: Two questions, two axes. `category` answers why a canonical route exists and which part of the projection it belongs to. `binding` answers whether Rust binds it and, when it does not, why not -- with evidence, and with a durable task when the reason is temporary. A purpose is never an answer to the binding question: 'this backs XNA' says nothing about whether the Rust projection reaches it. BOUND is measured from the reviewed cna-sys slice and is never declared here; every other status must be stated, and every statement must carry a reason and evidence a reader can check.

knownDefects.summary: a content-loaded Model's teardown faults: ~MeshResource moves an empty detachedValue over a loaded part's value, and ~PartResource dereferences it. Every route answers correctly; only teardown is affected, and leaking the handle moves the fault to process exit rather than avoiding it. The routes stay BOUND because they work -- this records the defect against them so the scoreboard is not the only thing a reader sees.

refuses a skin the content pipeline imported -- 'The Model skin's skeleton was not created through the C API' -- which is not the refusal the header documents. The route is bound and works for a skin added through cna_model_add_skin_ext.

rules.reason: cna_camera_create_with_test_backend_ext points CNA's global platform override at memory the camera handle owns, and cna_camera_destroy frees it without clearing the override, so any later camera query reads freed memory. Measured as SIGSEGV (wait status 139) from Rust; the baseline sequence without that query exits 0. Building a projection on a lifecycle that faults would mean hiding it.
rules.evidence: docs/upstream-findings.md#rust-upstream-020, crates/cna/tests/upstream_camera_destroy.rs

rules.reason: these build a native Model by hand, and crates/cna/src/graphics/model.rs already is the XNA Model in Rust: Model, ModelBone, ModelMesh, ModelMeshPart, their collections and enumerators, CopyAbsoluteBoneTransformsTo and Draw, built by this crate's own .xnb ModelReader and disposed through ContentDisposable. Binding these would put a second, weaker Model in the crate -- one whose parts are opaque handles rather than typed Rust values -- for callers who already have the real one. The read side of the same header is bound, because a model CNA loaded carries glTF facts the Rust reader cannot produce.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/graphics/model.rs, crates/cna/src/content/reader.rs (model_reader), crates/cna/tests/content_xnb.rs

rules.reason: this tag is an opaque 64-bit slot for a C caller's own pointer -- upstream calls it 'the C-owned opaque model tag' and never reads it. A Rust caller attaches data by keeping it in their own type, which is typed, borrow-checked and cannot outlive what it describes. The tag an asset actually carries is a different route, cna_model_get_content_tag_dictionary_ext, and that one is tracked rather than refused.
rules.evidence: models.h's own contrast between cna_model_get_tag and cna_model_get_content_tag_dictionary_ext: 'That one is a C-owned opaque value a caller sets and reads back; this one is what a custom ContentProcessor wrote into the .xnb'

rules.reason: XNA's ToString() formats, which Rust implements for each of these types with the same layout: Viewport::ToString, GamePadState::ToString, MouseState::ToString, TouchLocation::ToString, and the five sensor readings plus the legacy AccelerometerReadingEvent. Named one by one rather than by suffix on purpose -- the same routes exist for types Rust has no ToString for yet, and a wildcard here would quietly claim a fidelity this crate does not have.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/graphics/viewport.rs, crates/cna/src/input/gamepad.rs, crates/cna/src/input/mouse.rs, crates/cna/src/input/touch.rs, crates/cna/src/extensions/sensors.rs; each format was read off the matching cnanext ToString() rather than guessed

rules.reason: a TouchCollection is a list of small values, and crates/cna/src/input/touch.rs is that list: Add, Clear, Contains, CopyTo, IndexOf, Insert, RemoveAt, Count and IsReadOnly are all Rust, over a Rust Vec. The locations, the gesture samples and the capabilities are constructed the same way. What is *not* in this rule is cna_touch_panel_*, which reads and drives a device rather than a value, and is bound.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/input/touch.rs, whose collection semantics the behaviour corpus measures against XNA's documented IList rules

rules.reason: crates/cna/src/game/components.rs is the whole XNA component model in Rust -- GameComponent, DrawableGameComponent, IUpdateable, IDrawable, GameComponentCollection with its added/removed events -- and it makes no native call at all: zero `sys::` references in the file. The Rust Game loop is what drives it, through GameState's initialize_all, update_all and draw_all, so a component registered through the C collection would sit in a second list nothing iterates. Binding these would not add a capability; it would add a parallel component system that never runs. GameServiceContainer is the same, in crates/cna/src/game/services.rs.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/game/components.rs and crates/cna/src/game/state.rs, whose Update and Draw call the collection directly; the behaviour corpus measures component ordering against XNA's documented rules

rules.reason: these are pure value arithmetic, and cna::value implements each operation in Rust: Matrix::Invert, CreateLookAt and Decompose, Vector3::Normalize, Quaternion::Slerp, BoundingBox::Intersects, BoundingFrustum::Contains and Color::FromNonPremultiplied are Rust functions over Rust values. Binding the C route would put a second implementation of the same arithmetic behind a native call that can fail, and the two could disagree. Eleven curve routes are the exception and are bound: cnb_decode_curve answers a CNA_CurveHandle and cnb_encode_curve wants one, and a Curve is one of CNB's eight asset types, so without a way to build and read a native curve a Rust game could not load a curve asset at all. They are used for marshalling only -- create, destroy, the two loop modes, and the key collection -- and nothing that evaluates or computes tangents is bound, so the arithmetic is still Rust's.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/value/, and crates/cna/src/value/tests.rs which measures the Rust arithmetic against XNA's documented results

rules.reason: each of these makes a detached technique, pass, parameter or collection that a second call then adds somewhere. CNA also offers the combined form -- cna_effect_pass_collection_add_create, cna_effect_parameter_collection_add_create, cna_effect_technique_collection_add_named, cna_effect_annotation_collection_add -- and that is what this crate's Effect uses, because it cannot leave a half-built object stranded between the two calls. A detached technique that is never added has no use and no owner; binding the split form would add a way to leak one.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/graphics/effect.rs, whose apply_reflection_blueprint builds the whole graph through the add-create routes

rules.reason: a Viewport is six numbers and the operations over them are arithmetic: crates/cna/src/graphics/viewport.rs computes AspectRatio, Bounds, TitleSafeArea, Project and Unproject in Rust, including the perspective divide and its epsilon. The value never leaves Rust, so binding these would put a second implementation of the same arithmetic behind a native call that can fail -- the same reason the vectors and matrices are not bound.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/graphics/viewport.rs; the projection maths is measured against XNA's documented results in the behaviour corpus

rules.reason: a GamePadState is four small values and these construct or read them. crates/cna/src/input/gamepad.rs builds each with a Rust constructor -- GamePadDPad::new, GamePadTriggers::new with its own NaN-aware clamp, GamePadThumbSticks::new, GamePadState's from_... -- and reads them back through Buttons, DPad, ThumbSticks and Triggers. `is_pressed` is GamePadState::IsButtonDown. Binding these would put a fallible native call in front of a field read the compiler already checks. The routes that read a *device* rather than a value -- the touchpad, the motion sensors, the light bar -- are bound, because those are not values Rust holds. The packet-number setter is in the same rule: it writes a field into a caller's CNA_GamePadState, and Rust's GamePadState carries its own PacketNumber, read straight off the state CNA filled.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/input/gamepad.rs, and the behaviour corpus which measures the trigger clamp and the button mask against XNA's documented results

rules.reason: the reflective builder declares a field as a value kind and a byte offset -- 'where to store it in the object' -- and CNA then writes that many bytes into a pointer the caller's create callback returned. Nothing checks that the offset is inside the object or that the kind matches the field's type, so a caller who pairs offset_of!(T, an_i32) with the Matrix kind gets sixty-four bytes written over a four-byte field, from safe Rust. A wrapper cannot check either half. The capability is not lost: cna_content_type_reader_manager_register is the other extension point for a caller's own type, and it reads fields through a borrowed ContentReader rather than writing at offsets, which is the shape this crate already binds safely for .cnb loaders.
rules.evidence: content_readers.h's own wording for cna_reflective_type_reader_builder_add_field; crates/cna/src/extensions/content.rs, whose CnbLoader is the same extension point in the safe shape

rules.reason: XNA's Equals and GetHashCode exist because a .NET value type inherits object. Every Rust counterpart of these types derives PartialEq -- GamePadState, MouseState, KeyboardState, DisplayMode, SensorInfo, JoystickInfo, the sensor readings -- so `a == b` is the operation, the compiler checks it, and a HashMap key works without asking C anything. Where XNA's named methods matter for source fidelity the Rust types carry them too. Binding these would add a fallible native call that answers a question `==` has already answered, and the two could disagree.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/input/gamepad.rs, crates/cna/src/input/mod.rs, crates/cna/src/input/mouse.rs, crates/cna/src/input/touch.rs, crates/cna/src/extensions/sensors.rs -- every type these routes name derives PartialEq, and TouchLocation, KeyboardState and the GamePad* types also spell XNA's own Equals and GetHashCode

rules.reason: these are XNA's constructors reached through C: cna_viewport_init is ToC(Viewport()) and cna_gamepad_state_init_from_values is the parameterised constructor. Rust builds these values with Default, a `new`, or a struct literal, none of which can fail. The descriptor structs that carry struct_size and struct_version are filled at the call site with size_of and the version the header states, and tools/native-abi/verify.py probes every layout against the headers -- so the field-setting these routes exist to get right is already checked by a stronger mechanism than a runtime call.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/graphics/viewport.rs, crates/cna/src/input/gamepad.rs, crates/cna/src/graphics/presentation.rs; tools/native-abi/verify.py's layoutTypesProbed, which checks every descriptor's field order and offsets against the canonical headers

rules.reason: these answer .NET's GetType().Name, and upstream's implementations are all compile-time constants -- every GetTypeName() in cnanext returns a fixed string such as 'Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Input.KeyboardState'. A Rust caller knows the type statically at every call site, so there is no reflection question to ask, and the .NET name of a Rust value is not a fact about that value. The one place these strings genuinely matter is the content format, where the reader name is part of the .xnb, and the crate already carries them as data in AssetTypeId rather than fetching them one object at a time. Both spellings of the size half are covered: some families call it `_get_type_name_size` and some `_get_type_name_byte_count`, and binding one because the wildcard happened to miss the other is how an accessor with no caller gets into the crate.
rules.evidence: cnanext modules/*/src/Xna/*.cpp -- every GetTypeName() is a constant; crates/cna/src/content/reader.rs, which names the canonical readers directly

rules.reason: a KeyboardState is a 256-bit set, and crates/cna/src/input/mod.rs is that set: KeyboardState::new builds one from a slice of Keys and Item answers a slot, both over the same bit words CNA uses, with a to_native that hands the identical struct back for the routes that do need CNA. Binding these two would round-trip a value through C to compute what the bits already say. What is *not* in this rule is every _ext route in the same header: those ask the platform's live layout which key a scancode produces and what each is called, which no Rust code can answer, and they are bound. Nor is cna_keyboard_state_copy_string, which is CNA's ToString and is bound because the string is CNA's choice rather than the bit set's.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/tests/extensions_keyboard_layout.rs measures the bound half against the live library, including that a snapshot Rust built is one CNA's own value routes accept

rules.reason: each of these asks a snapshot a question the snapshot already answers in Rust: KeyboardState::IsKeyUp and GetPressedKeys over the same 256 bits CNA sets, GamePadState::IsButtonDown/IsButtonUp over the same button mask, TouchCollection::FindById and TouchLocation::TryGetPreviousLocation over the collection this side owns. The snapshots are read from CNA -- cna_keyboard_get_state, cna_gamepad_get_state, cna_touch_panel_get_state are all bound -- so the values are CNA's; only the querying is Rust's, and routing a query back through C would cost a call to learn what the bits in hand already say. What is *not* in this rule is cna_gamepad_apply_dead_zone, which is CNA's canonical clamping algorithm over raw values rather than a question about a snapshot, and is bound.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/input/mod.rs, gamepad.rs and touch.rs; the behaviour corpus measures each against XNA's documented answers

rules.reason: a MouseState is five integers and five button flags, and crates/cna/src/input/mouse.rs already constructs one from exactly those values. The snapshots a game reads come from CNA through the bound cna_mouse_get_state; this route only builds a value, and building it in Rust costs nothing and loses nothing. Every _ext route in the same header that reads or drives the actual device -- relative mode, capture, the desktop position, the warp, the clicked event and its test hooks -- is bound.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/input/mouse.rs; crates/cna/tests/extensions_mouse_desktop.rs qualifies the bound half against the live library

rules.reason: RUST-UPSTREAM-027. crates/cna/src/audio.rs already implements XNA's two static helpers and does it faithfully, down to the mixed binary32/double precision that makes one mono second at 44.1 kHz 88,198 bytes rather than 88,200. CNA's routes for the same two questions do not agree with XNA: the duration truncates where XNA's TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds rounds -- up to a millisecond short, and zero for a 100-byte stereo buffer at 44.1 kHz that XNA says lasts one -- and the size drops XNA's `num + num % Channels` frame alignment and does the rate division in double rather than binary32. Nineteen of ninety duration cases and fifteen of fifty size cases disagree. Binding these would replace a correct answer with a wrong one, which is the one thing a coverage number is not worth.
rules.evidence: docs/upstream-findings.md RUST-UPSTREAM-027; the decompiled XNA AudioFormat.DurationFromSize and SizeFromDuration are the arbiter; tools/reproducers/ext015q_sample_math.c prints CNA's answers and crates/cna/tests/extensions_audio_ext.rs pins the Rust ones to the reference values

rules.reason: RUST-EXT-017. These are worth binding and are not yet, because binding them alone would paper over a defect in the Rust projection rather than expose it. Measured: WaveBankState::dispose_xact_child and SoundBankState's equivalent call the low-level dispose, which destroys the handle without emitting the Rust `disposing` event -- so a handler registered through WaveBank::AddDisposingHandler does NOT fire when the engine that owns the bank is disposed, which is exactly when XNA's own Disposing fires. CNA raises its event on that path. Binding the native subscription would make the two disagree visibly, which is better than the silence there is now, but the fix is to make the Rust event fire and bind the native one as the cross-check in the same slice.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/audio/xact.rs: the `disposing.emit` calls are on the public Dispose paths (lines 136, 218) and not on the XactChild teardown path the engine drives

rules.reason: these three take a CNA_VertexDeclarationHandle, and the Rust VertexDeclaration has no native handle at all: crates/cna/src/graphics/vertex.rs keeps its elements and stride in Rust and hands them to CNA by value through native_elements() whenever a buffer is created. There is nothing on this side to call them with. Creating a native declaration purely so they could be called would add a second declaration beside the one that already works, with a lifetime to manage and no capability gained. What is NOT in this rule is cna_vertex_buffer_copy_declaration_elements, which reads the declaration a *buffer* was created with -- a buffer does have a handle, and a tool describing a buffer it did not create has no other route to its layout -- and that one is bound.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/graphics/vertex.rs, whose DeclarationState holds only disposed/name/tag/disposing and no handle; crates/cna/tests/extensions_device_surface.rs reads a buffer's layout back through the route that is bound
